source: Miro-Lopez-Feliu et al. (2026) Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics
finding: Models almost never say a task has no valid plan. They write a plan anyway. Wrong abstention on solvable tasks is almost absent, so the weakness is recall, not precision.
numbers: 50 tasks (5 domains, 8 solvable and 2 unsolvable each), 4 non-reasoning models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash and Flash-Lite). Only 32 of 360 unsolvable episodes ended in a detection (8.9%): 22 of 240 offline, 10 of 120 online. Best configuration found 4 of the 10 unsolvable tasks. The Critic architecture found none. 13 of the 22 offline detections came from one Gripper task. Only 1 of 1,440 solvable episodes falsely claimed no plan exists.
quote: Systems tend to attempt a plan rather than abstain (paraphrase of the paper)
limits: Small benchmark, one run per configuration at temperature 0, non-reasoning models. Unsolvable tasks are small edits of solvable ones. The prompt offers an explicit UNSOLVABLE flag.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answered for planning tasks: a no-valid-decomposition exit is almost never used by default, so it cuts few wrong answers unless the scaffold forces a feasibility check. Raising false refusals is not the risk at current settings (1 of 1,440).

source: Miro-Lopez-Feliu et al. (2026) Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics
finding: Subgoal-sketch prompting (Plan-and-Solve, a light decomposition) gave no gain that survived correction. Chain-of-thought alone did as well or better. Heavier scaffolds cost far more tokens.
numbers: Success on 40 solvable offline tasks, per model, Direct / CoT / Plan-and-Solve: GPT-4o-mini 12.5 / 27.5 / 17.5; GPT-4o 57.5 / 77.5 / 75.0; Flash-Lite 25.0 / 22.5 / 22.5; Flash 45.0 / 62.5 / 57.5. Mean tokens (thousands, 4-model average): Direct 1.5, CoT 4.3, Plan-and-Solve 2.9, Self-Refine 7.1, Tree of Thoughts 32.3 (about 22x Direct). No difference survives Holm correction; three are significant before it.
limits: Planning with known operators, not open reasoning. 40 tasks gives power only for large effects. Plan-and-Solve here writes 4 to 10 subgoals; it is not method-based decomposition.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 2: on non-reasoning models a plain decomposition step is not clearly better than CoT at similar tokens. Test any O3 gain against a CoT baseline with matched tokens.

source: Miro-Lopez-Feliu et al. (2026) Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics
finding: Planning failures are mostly illegal steps (precondition violations), not wrong goals. Acting online without checking state makes it worse.
numbers: 46-64% of plans for solvable tasks contain an inapplicable action under every prompting strategy, and those plans make up 89% of failed ones. Executable plans that miss the goal: 2.5-9%. Online, the best config (GPT-4o ReAct) solves 40.0% (16/40) vs 77.5% offline. Only 7.3% of online actions followed a state query. Precondition violations ended 66-68% of solvable online episodes.
limits: Deterministic, fully observable toy domains. Measures leaf legality, not decomposition quality.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly answered outside web tasks: the bottleneck sits at step legality (leaf precondition errors). Supports a mechanical check after each step and a state check before acting.

source: Miro-Lopez-Feliu et al. (2026) Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics
finding: Reflection and critic loops did not beat plain ReAct and added cost and timeouts. This is cost evidence against per-step verification by an LLM critic.
numbers: The Critic leaves precondition violations at 66% of solvable episodes (ReAct 67%) but timeouts rise to 15.0% vs 0.6%, because each rejected proposal uses a call. Critic uses 1.8x ReAct tokens (45.1k vs 25.6k mean); Reflexion 1.1x. Smallest uncorrected p for Reflexion or Critic vs ReAct is 0.25. An online episode costs $0.031 vs $0.007 offline. Every Pareto-front configuration (score vs cost) is offline.
limits: The paper notes LLM self-critique of plan semantics is unreliable, so the critic only sees mechanical issues. A formal validator (VAL) is far cheaper than an LLM critic.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: verification pays when it is a cheap mechanical check. An LLM critic about doubled tokens here for no measured gain. Prefer code validators for postconditions.

source: Fan, Li, Sun, Zhou (2025) Missing Premise exacerbates Overthinking: Are Reasoning Models losing Critical Thinking Skill?
finding: Reasoning models given ill-posed questions (a needed premise is deleted) think far longer and rarely say the question is ill-posed. Non-reasoning models answer shorter and flag the problem more often.
numbers: Datasets: MiP-Formula (50 synthetic), MiP-SVAMP, MiP-GSM8K (582), MiP-MATH (58). On MiP-GSM8K, DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-32B used over 3,000 tokens on MiP questions vs about 1,000 on well-defined ones; non-reasoning models stayed near 200 tokens for both. Abstain rate on MiP-GSM8K, read from Figure 2: non-reasoning models roughly 44-56%; reasoning models roughly 10-40% (QwQ-32B about 10% at 4,780 tokens). On MiP-MATH abstention is low for all models.
quote: Reasoning LLMs produce much longer responses to ill-posed questions lacking a necessary premise (abstract, paraphrase)
limits: The Table 2 text layout was garbled in extraction, so the pairing of numbers to models is uncertain; ranges are from Figure 2 and the table together. Abstain is judged by an LLM. Models are early 2025 (R1, QwQ, o1 family).
agent_relevance: Gap 4: extra thinking does not buy a no-valid-answer exit. A scaffold needs an explicit missing-premise check before decomposing, and a token cap when it fails.

source: Sun, Wang, Song et al. (2026) Agent Planning Benchmark: A Diagnostic Framework for Planning Capabilities in LLM Agents
finding: On a 4,209-case planning benchmark, frontier multimodal models refuse impossible tasks well when the impossibility is a stated contradiction, but poorly when information or a tool is silently missing. They fill the gap by guessing.
numbers: 12 MLLMs. Refusal rate (%) by infeasibility type, Constraint conflict / Missing information / Tool removal / Visual missing: GPT-5 80/40/75/89; Gemini 3 Pro 65/43/65/16; Claude Sonnet 4.5 72/19/16/53; Gemini 2.5 Pro 77/65/75/11; GPT-4o 78/39/30/64; Qwen3VL-235B 72/11/7/64. Step-wise correctness rate: Gemini 3 Pro 80.1, GPT-5 77.4, Sonnet 4.5 77.3.
quote: models handle explicit Constraint Conflict far better than Information Missing (paraphrase)
limits: Multimodal tool-use planning, not text reasoning. Judged by an LLM. The false-refusal rate on solvable tasks was not reported in the text read.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: confabulating a plan when information is missing is common even in frontier models (refusal 7-65% on missing info or tools). A no-valid-decomposition exit should check for missing information and tools by name, not only contradictions.

source: Sun et al. (2026) Agent Planning Benchmark, refinement and horizon results
finding: Critic-guided refinement of a whole plan helps a lot. Refinement of step-by-step decisions helps little or hurts. Plans get worse as the planned horizon grows.
numbers: Taxonomy-guided critic refinement lifted InternVL3.5-241B holistic correctness from 22.00% to 60.00%. Extending the prediction scope from 1 to 3 steps lowered correctness for all models. Extraneous tools cut holistic accuracy by 22.0 points (GPT-5) and 12.3 (Sonnet 4.5) but only 0.9-6.7 in step-wise mode. On ToolSandbox, executed similarity for GPT-4o went from 76.3 (direct) to 79.2 (plan-first) to 83.3 (refined).
limits: Authors' own error taxonomy and critic; refinement token cost not read. Mostly multimodal tool use.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 3: a taxonomy-guided check on a full plan is a verification with a large measured gain, but step-wise replanning already uses feedback and extra reflection can over-correct. Gate extra checks on whether feedback is already in the loop.

source: SCOPE authors (2025) SCOPE: Language Models as One-Time Teacher for Hierarchical Planning in Text Environments (ADaPT re-run with other backends)
finding: ADaPT's as-needed decomposition was re-run with newer backends on TextCraft. The result plateaus near 0.58 for strong models and collapses for weak or format-fragile ones. The benefit does not vanish with GPT-4o-class models, but it depends on the executor.
numbers: TextCraft success for ADaPT by backend: GPT-4o 0.58; Mistral Small 3 (24B) 0.58; GPT-3.5 0.52 (original); GPT-4o mini 0.43; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 0.13; Claude-3 Haiku 0.00. ADaPT took 164.4 s per game with GPT-3.5 vs 3.0 s for the 11M-parameter student SCOPE (0.56).
limits: No no-decomposition baseline for the same backends is in this table, so the ADaPT gain over plain ReAct on these models is not isolated. SCOPE authors are competitors. Newest backend is GPT-4o (2024); no Claude 4 or GPT-5 class model.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed: gating on failure still works for GPT-4o-class models, but its value over a plain agent at frontier level is untested. Keep the gate cheap and verify the executor obeys the output format.

source: SCOPE (2025), hand-engineered vs LLM-generated subgoals
finding: In a fixed domain, hand-written subgoals worked as well as LLM-proposed ones after the planner was fine-tuned. Without the second training stage performance dropped sharply.
numbers: TextCraft success: SCOPE with LLM subgoals 0.56; with hand-engineered subgoals 0.58; without manager fine-tuning 0.24.
limits: One domain (TextCraft), a trained 11M-parameter student, not a prompted frontier model. It does not test a method library given in the prompt.
agent_relevance: Gap 1, weak support: in a closed crafting domain a hand-written subgoal set equals model-proposed subgoals (0.58 vs 0.56). Not a test on natural reasoning tasks.

source: Choi, Kim, Ong et al. (2026) ReAcTree: Hierarchical LLM Agent Trees with Control Flow for Long-Horizon Task Planning
finding: A tree of subgoal agents beat a flat ReAct agent on long household tasks. The gain was largest with good examples, and it reversed for a small model with poor examples.
numbers: WAH-NL (long-horizon). Qwen 2.5 72B goal success rate (GSR): ReAct+WM 31% vs ReAcTree+WM 61%; subgoal success rate 54.05% vs 79.58%. No-memory 72B: ReAct 13% vs ReAcTree 31%. No-memory Qwen 2.5 7B: ReAct 7.00% vs ReAcTree 2.00% (reversal). ALFRED valid-unseen GSR with LLaMA 3.1 70B: 32.40 vs 37.03; with LLaMA 3.1 8B: 19.61 vs 26.19. Tokens per decision were similar across methods.
limits: Open-weight models only (LLaMA 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Phi-4); no frontier or reasoning model. Embodied household tasks, not open reasoning. Authors' own baselines.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 6: decomposition gains hold with 70B-class open models at similar per-decision tokens, but a weak model without good examples is hurt by decomposition. Gate decomposition on model strength and example quality.

source: Choi et al. (2026) ReAcTree control-flow ablation
finding: Letting the tree try an alternative when a subgoal fails (fallback), and run parts in parallel, mattered a lot. A plain sequence of subgoals lost much of the gain.
numbers: GSR (%) by control flow, LLaMA 3.1 8B / 70B, Qwen 2.5 7B / 72B: all flows 30 / 58 / 37 / 61; sequence+fallback 28 / 58 / 38 / 61; sequence only 18 / 36 / 15 / 46.
limits: Control flow is tree structure, not method ordering inside a library. One benchmark (WAH-NL).
agent_relevance: Gap 10: an alternative-on-failure path (the SHOP2 'ordered alternatives' idea) is worth about 10-22 points of GSR. Ordering inside the alternatives was not varied. Supports building fallback into O3.

source: Li, Liu, Chen et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks
finding: Giving agents a curated package of procedures raised pass rates a lot on average, with large spread across domains. This is the closest direct test of a given method library vs none on realistic tasks.
numbers: 87 tasks, 8 domains, 18 model-harness configurations, 3 trials each, deterministic verifiers. No skills 33.9% vs curated skills 50.5% (+16.6 points; 25.5% normalised); per configuration +4.1 to +25.7. By domain: Natural Science 42.0 to 70.8 (+28.8); Cybersecurity +14.2; Software Engineering +11.6; Mathematics and OR +9.7. 13 of 87 tasks had negative deltas (worst -7.4).
limits: Skills are agent-harness packages (instructions plus scripts), not HTN methods. Tokens and cost were not equalised: the skill text adds input. Tasks are terminal tasks with verifiers, not pure reasoning.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a given library helps on realistic multi-domain tasks, most where pretraining is thin, less where the model is strong (math, software). An equal-token comparison is still missing.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench, self-generated skills
finding: When the agent writes its own skill packs before solving, results are worse than no skills. A model-improvised library is not a substitute for a curated one.
numbers: Self-generated skills vs no skills: -8.1 points (Claude Code + Opus 4.7), -11.3 (Codex + GPT-5.5), -11.5 (Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro). Curated skills on the same three: +18.2 to +24.8. Audit of 12 trajectories: on two harnesses 10 of 12 never read the generated skills; in one, authoring used up the run; one generated pack hard-coded a wrong unit assumption.
quote: Self-generated Skills land below the no-Skills baseline on all three configurations (paper text)
limits: The audit is 12 trajectories. Creator and solver share one context in one harness, which confounds. The authors keep this condition as a diagnostic, not the main result.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 5: unverified self-written method libraries can hurt. A growing library needs verification before reuse and a check that the solver actually uses it.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench, design ablations
finding: More skills and longer skills were not better. A few compact procedures did best. This bears on library size and conflicts.
numbers: Gain by number of skills per task: 1 skill +18.0 points; 2-3 skills +19.0; 4 or more +10.1. Gain by skill length: compact +19.0, standard +21.5, detailed +14.5, comprehensive +0.7. A small model with skills (MiniMax M2.7, 34.9%) beat stronger no-skill baselines (32.7% and 29.7%). Negative deltas came from a single 'correct' pipeline with no applicability limits or fallbacks.
limits: Observational split by existing task skill sets, not randomised library sizes.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 10: keep the method set per task small (about 1-3) and give each method applicability conditions and a fallback. Large libraries add conflict and overhead.

source: Wang, Gandhi, Neubig, Fried (2025) Inducing Programmatic Skills for Agentic Tasks (ASI)
finding: Skills induced from the agent's own runs and checked by executing them improved WebArena success and cut steps. Execution-based verification was a measurable part of the gain.
numbers: WebArena success with Claude 3.5 Sonnet: static 32.7, AWM (text skills, no execution check) 36.3, ASI 40.4. Steps 5.6 / 5.9 / 5.0. Ablation on the shopping site: unverified text skills 32.6; verified program skills kept in memory 36.4; verified text 39.0; verified programs as actions 40.1. Only 15.6% of ASI induction turns passed verification, vs 31.4% of turns where AWM added skills.
limits: Web tasks, one backbone, authors' baselines. Verification is a run plus an LLM evaluator, which can pass wrong skills. Library stayed small.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 2: verified induction gave +3.8 to +7.5 points over unverified on the shopping site, at the price of rejecting about 84% of induction attempts. Verification was cheap relative to the gain.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) SkillWeaver: Web Agents can Self-Improve by Discovering and Honing Skills
finding: Agents that practice, synthesise and test reusable API skills improve over a practice stream. Skills from a strong agent transfer to a weaker one.
numbers: 160 iterations of the three-stage pipeline. WebArena average success, GPT-4o 22.6 to 29.8 (+31.8% relative); GPT-4o-mini 9.2 to 14.1. Real sites (Online-Mind2Web): 40.2 to 56.2 average (+39.8%); Car site unchanged at 11.1; Flight 11.7 to 29.4. Skills from GPT-4o raised weaker agents by up to 54.3% on WebArena.
limits: Skills are short single-call APIs, per website. Authors' own harness. Staleness and conflict between skills were not measured.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: growth from verified practice helps over a stream of about 160 practice iterations, with uneven gains (none on one site). Not yet shown at a few hundred mixed reasoning items.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) SkillWeaver, limitation of the verification test
finding: A weak check lets bad skills into the library. Skills counted as verified if the call raised no exception, so some broken skills passed by swallowing errors.
numbers: Appendix D.2.1: functions were marked verified 'simply because they silenced all exceptions'. The LLM added if-guards that avoided errors without making the function work.
limits: Qualitative case; no rate given.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 2: the postcondition check for a verified decomposition must test the outcome, not the absence of an error.

source: Gui et al. (2025) HyperTree Planning, comparison with o1-preview
finding: Against a reasoning model, the task-tree scaffold on a standard model won on two constraint-planning benchmarks at much lower cost, but lost badly on Blocksworld.
numbers: Success rate (cost per instance). TravelPlanner: o1-preview 10.0 ($0.38), GPT-4o 4.4, GPT-4o+HTP 20.0 ($0.071), Gemini-1.5-Pro+HTP 36.1 ($0.102). Trip planning: o1-preview 31.1, GPT-4o+HTP 36.9, Gemini+HTP 42.8; the paper says HTP matches or beats o1-preview at 8.7-13% of its cost. Blocksworld: o1-preview 97.8 ($0.42), GPT-4o+HTP 54.8, Gemini+HTP 67.2. HTP tokens on TravelPlanner 5,562 in and 963 out vs CoT 4,328 and 641.
limits: Cost is dollars, not equal tokens. o1-preview is a 2024 reasoning model, not a current frontier one. HTP was not run on a reasoning model. The cost column in the extracted table is partly misaligned.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed: a task-tree scaffold can beat an early reasoning model on constraint satisfaction at lower cost, but not on Blocksworld. Untested against current reasoning models at equal tokens.

source: Alford, Kuter, Nau (2009) Translating HTNs to PDDL: A small amount of domain knowledge can go a long way (IJCAI-09)
finding: Method knowledge, even partial and incomplete, compiled into PDDL sped up a general planner (Fast-Forward) by orders of magnitude. The planner still chose among applicable methods.
numbers: Over 3,500 random problems in three domains (100 runs per point, 2-hour limit). Towers of Hanoi 3-14 rings: about 2 orders of magnitude faster at 14 rings. Blocks World 5-90 blocks (1,800 problems): plain FF times out as size grows. Office Delivery with up to 90 rooms and 90 packages (1,700 problems): 2.8 and 1.9 orders of magnitude faster. In Blocks World two methods stayed applicable at every step and the planner heuristic chose.
quote: such knowledge speeded up the well-known Fast-Forward planner by several orders of magnitude
limits: Needs restricted (totally ordered simple task network) HTNs. Classical planning, not LLMs. Does not address the Lekavy-Navrat critique itself.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 1: partial method libraries pay off even when search still picks among alternatives, so the scaffold does not need complete methods. HTN methods compile into goal-style planning, so the expressivity dispute matters little for design.

source: Wikipedia, 'Hierarchical task network' (read 2026-11-01)
finding: The current article says HTN planning is strictly more expressive than STRIPS and undecidable in general (citing Erol, Hendler, Nau 1996), and that some HTNs compile to PDDL (Alford 2009). It does not mention Lekavy or Navrat, so their critique could not be checked here.
numbers: Three sources are cited for expressivity: Erol, Hendler, Nau 1996 (Ann. Math. AI 18: 69-93); Alford, Bercher, Aha 2015; Alford, Kuter, Nau 2009.
limits: Wikipedia is a secondary source. Semantic Scholar searches for the Lekavy and Navrat paper returned nothing, and search quotas were exhausted, so the full text was not found.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. A safe design reading: HTN gains in expressive power need unbounded or variable task labels, which a scaffold with depth limits does not use.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (comment on Shojaee et al.)
finding: The reported collapse of reasoning models on Tower of Hanoi, even with an algorithm given, is partly an output-length artefact. Some River Crossing instances in the original were impossible, so scoring them as failures was wrong.
numbers: Full move lists of 2^N-1 moves at about 10 tokens each exceed output limits at modest N, matching the reported collapse near N=8 to 9. A preliminary run asking for a recursive function instead of a move list gave very high accuracy on N=15 for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3 and Gemini 2.5, in under 5,000 tokens (no exact score table). River Crossing with N of 6 or more and boat capacity 3 is mathematically impossible.
limits: Short comment, run by the comment's author, preliminary, no full numbers. It raises, but does not settle, whether the collapse is real.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: supports letting the model emit a compact rule or function and holding the step list in code, as K19 suggests. Confirms the need to flag impossible instances (gap 4).

source: Choi et al. (2026) ReAcTree memory ablation (subgoal-level examples)
finding: Retrieved subgoal-level example trajectories (a library built from successful runs) gave large gains for flat and tree agents alike. Example quality mattered more for small models.
numbers: Qwen 2.5 72B GSR with episodic plus working memory: ReAct 31% (no memory 13%, +18); ReAcTree 61% (no memory 31%, +30). Episodic memory only for ReAct: +13 points (26%). Episodic memory was bootstrapped from successful trajectories of LLaMA 3.1 70B plus one manual trajectory per task type. The authors report that without episodic retrieval the 7B model gets a fixed, mismatched example and does worse with extra working memory.
limits: Small memory built from one training set, one benchmark, no staleness study.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 5: retrieved successful sub-solutions are worth about +13 to +30 points here, and a mismatched example can hurt a weak model.
